I need to buy oil + a whetstone to keep my kitchen knives sharp. Any recommendations?

$23:

[Search Amazon.com for "Lansky Standard Coarse Sharpening System with Fine Hones"]

You can use water instead of oil BTW, it works just as well and makes much less mess.

I just use a Norton oilstone (sacrilege, I know) and the coarse side. I've tried lots of different methods, and this works best for me. There are lots of YouTube videos, and they recommend everything from power belt sanders to expensive sharpening systems. The one that seemed to work the best for me was to sharpen both sides equally freehand, and use an angle that measures about half of your index finger. The biggest key is to make sure that the edge is equal on both sides.

I use the stone dry or with water, and my knives are always sharp. The only gripe I have about the Norton stone is that it has no handle, so I may correct that at some point (My stone is 8-10" long, so it's not tough to hold).

Another way is to buy a flat diamond stone and epoxy it to a piece of wood molding as a handle. That probably works even better, though the diamond does need to be cleaned every so often.

Both methods are about $10 for the "stones," plus whatever it costs you to affix them to a good holder. You need a coarse sharpening stone. The fine ones take forever, and you don't get a good cutting edge for meats.

YMMV, of course, and I will no doubt be "flamed" for saying this, but my knives are plenty sharp. Can I shave with them? Don't know. Not enough hair on my arms, and any other hair is connected to parts too sensitive to subject them to testing...

I once had two identical kitchen knives and conducted a test with them - the first was sharpened as well as I could manage, and finished using my fine stone. The second was sharpened using only the coarsest stone I had. Then I used them both in the kitchen for a few weeks.

To my great surprise they cut identically well and the coarse knife seems to hold its edge a bit longer. This was all vegetables and meats, slicing and chopping. The coarse knife would not push-cut worth a damn but I never do that in the kitchen anyway.

It turns out that microserrations work pretty nice for slicing food. Even tomatoes.
